title: The standard error of the primary-on-primary estimate
published: The average estimated primary-on-general CACE is 0.0086 (SE = 0.0236), while the average estimated primary-on-primary CACE is 0.0068 (SE=[[0.0010]]).
corrected: The average estimated primary-on-general CACE is 0.0086 (SE = 0.0236), while the average estimated primary-on-primary CACE is 0.0068 (SE=[[0.0099]]).
note: The estimate and the other three figures in the sentence reproduce exactly. As printed, a standard error of 0.0010 would put the primary-on-primary estimate 6.8 standard errors from zero, which contradicts the sentence's own point that inducement to vote in a primary has negligible downstream effects. Recomputed, the estimate is 0.69 standard errors from zero, and is indistinguishable from zero as the passage says.

title: Battleground status among the strongest presidential-on-presidential estimates
published: The top panel of Table 5, for example, reports 15 estimates of the presidential-on-presidential downstream effect for 2008--12. The top [[four]] of the five strongest estimates (Arkansas, Nevada, Connecticut, Missouri, and New Jersey) are found in nonbattleground states.
corrected: The top panel of Table 5, for example, reports 15 estimates of the presidential-on-presidential downstream effect for 2008--12. The top [[three]] of the five strongest estimates (Arkansas, Nevada, Connecticut, Missouri, and New Jersey) are found in nonbattleground states.
note: Under the article's own coding, a state is a presidential battleground when the two-party vote share difference in the downstream election is ten points or fewer. Nevada at 6.8 points and Missouri at 9.6 points clear that threshold in 2012, so three of the five strongest estimates are in nonbattleground states rather than four. Ten of the fifteen states with a 2008-12 estimate are nonbattleground, so 3.33 of the five strongest are expected to be nonbattleground by chance alone; three is the modal outcome, at p = 0.40, and the published four or more occurs 43 percent of the time. The corrected count is what chance gives, which is what the passage asserts two sentences earlier: "In fact, we see little difference."

note: Every standard error in the discontinuity tables is heteroskedasticity-robust, and the deposited code computes it as coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovHC) on a two-stage least squares fit from the AER package. The sandwich package carries no leverage convention of its own: it calls hatvalues() on the fit it is handed. AER's method for a 2SLS fit returns the diagonal of the asymmetric matrix that maps the outcome onto its fitted values, and Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch (1980) considered exactly that quantity for 2SLS diagnostics and recommended against it, on the ground that the diagonal of an asymmetric matrix is not a leverage. The ivreg package, which now carries the implementation AER once did, follows that recommendation and uses the second-stage projection, whose diagonal lies between zero and one by construction. The maintained pipeline follows the later convention. On the Iowa 2004-06 pair the two give 0.048544 and 0.048498, either side of the boundary at which the third decimal turns. The difference runs to about a part in a thousand, so the published figure stands at the precision these tables print in 926 of 937 cells. The eleven that move are of two kinds. Three are a single state's own standard error, each sitting on a rounding boundary. The other eight are pooled quantities that inherit those standard errors through a weight: Table 6's meta-analytic estimate is precision-weighted by them, Table 7's models are weighted by their inverse squares, and every cell of appendix Tables A6 and A7 is a fixed-effects meta-analysis across the same states, whose weights are the same standard errors. That is how the convention reaches a point estimate, which each state's own estimate is immune to. No sentence in the article or the appendix quotes any of the eleven. The appendix's six sit in the tables its Section 2 offers as evidence that the estimates are quite robust to specification, and the corrected values leave that reading exactly where it was: the 2008-on-2012 estimates still cluster between 0.10 and 0.12, the 2006-on-2010 estimates still fall mostly between 0.07 and 0.15, and the standard errors still shrink as the window widens.
